questions.text: Which one of the following statements is TRUE for all positive functions [latex]f(n)[/latex]?
questions.solution:
Checking each option:
- Polynomial [latex]f(n)=n^k[/latex]: [latex]f(n^2)=n^{2k}[/latex] and [latex]f(n)^2=n^{2k}[/latex], so [latex]f(n^2)=\Theta(f(n)^2)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]f(n^2)=o(f(n)^2)[/latex] fails for polynomials (they are equal, not strictly smaller).
- For [latex]f(n)=2^n[/latex]: [latex]f(n^2)=2^{n^2}[/latex] but [latex]f(n)^2=2^{2n}[/latex]; [latex]2^{n^2}[/latex] grows much faster, so [latex]O[/latex] fails.
- For [latex]f(n)=2^{-n}[/latex]: [latex]f(n^2)=2^{-n^2}[/latex] is much smaller than [latex]f(n)^2=2^{-2n}[/latex], so [latex]\Omega[/latex] fails.

Answer: [latex]f(n^2)=\Theta(f(n)^2)[/latex], where f(n) is a polynomial

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: [latex]f(n^2)=\theta (f(n)^2)[/latex], where [latex]f(n)[/latex] is a polynomial
[latex]f(n^2)=o (f(n)^2)[/latex]
[latex]f(n^2)=O (f(n)^2)[/latex], where [latex]f(n)[/latex] is an exponential function
[latex]f(n^2)=\Omega  (f(n)^2)[/latex]

questions.text: Which one of the following regular expressions correctly represents the language of the finite automaton given below?
questions.solution:
The start state is not final. From start:
- on a go to the upper final state (loops on b, returns to start on b) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] one round trip is [latex]ab^*b[/latex];
- on b go to the lower final state (loops on a, returns to start on a) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] one round trip is [latex]ba^*a[/latex].

So: any number of round trips [latex](ab^*b+ba^*a)^*[/latex], and then finish in one of the final states: [latex]ab^*[/latex] or [latex]ba^*[/latex].

Answer: [latex](ba^*a+ab^*b)^*(ab^*+ba^*)[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: ab*bab* + ba*aba*
(ab*b)*ab* + (ba*a)*ba*
(ab*b + ba*a)*(a* + b*)
(ba*a + ab*b)*(ab* + ba*)

questions.text: Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- LALR(1) merges LR(1) states with the same core; this merging can create a new reduce-reduce conflict [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- The symbol table is used in almost every phase (semantic analysis, code generation, [latex]\ldots[/latex]) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Data flow analysis is used for code optimization, not run-time memory management [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Every deterministic CFL has an LR(1) grammar, so LR(1) parsing is sufficient for DCFLs [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: LR(1) parsing is sufficient for deterministic context-free languages

questions.text: In a relational data model, which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Relation R(A, B): the only possible non-trivial FDs are [latex]A\rightarrow B[/latex] or [latex]B\rightarrow A[/latex]. In each case the left side is a key, so R is always in BCNF [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- All attributes prime guarantees 3NF, not BCNF (e.g. [latex]AB\rightarrow C,\ C\rightarrow B[/latex]) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- A relation can have no non-prime attribute (e.g. all attributes form the key) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- BCNF decomposition does not always preserve FDs [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: A relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: A relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF.
If all attributes of a relation are prime attributes, then the relation is in BCNF.
Every relation has at least one non-prime attribute.
BCNF decompositions preserve functional dependencies.

questions.text:
Consider the problem of reversing a singly linked list. To take an example, given the linked list below,

the reversed linked list should look like

Which one of the following statements is TRUE about the time complexity of algorithms that solve the above problem in O(1) space?
questions.solution:
Walk the list once with three pointers (prev, curr, next), reversing each link as you go:
next = curr[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]next; curr[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next.

Each node is visited once and only 3 extra pointers are used, so it takes [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] time in [latex]O(1)[/latex] space. It cannot be faster, because every link must be changed.

Answer: The best algorithm takes [latex]\theta(n)[/latex] time in the worst case

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: The best algorithm for the problem takes [latex]\theta(n)[/latex] time in the worst case.
The best algorithm for the problem takes [latex]\theta(n \log n)[/latex] time in the worst case.
The best algorithm for the problem takes [latex]\theta(n^2)[/latex] time in the worst case.
It is not possible to reverse a singly linked list in O(1) space.
